summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

Follow-up on PR #391 (branch review-fix/391, your worktree): the maintainer decided lead (b) — implement the fallback. When DDL projected out of a PL/pgSQL DO body is rejected by the grammar (e.g. `CREATE TEMP TABLE … ON COMMIT DROP AS`, `DEFAULT r.name`), the file must NOT fail: fall back to masking that DO block whole, as origin/main does, so a file that parses cleanly on main keeps parsing cleanly. The maintainer's reasoning: a file-level failure caused by a projected DO body helps nobody.
Requirements: (1) the fallback is per DO block where feasible (a good block in the same file still has its DDL projected); if only per-file fallback is practical, do that and say so; (2) it must not be a fully silent drop — if the codebase has a suitable existing warning mechanism (a warning record, not a partial failure), emit one naming the file; if adding one would need a new diagnostic code (schema-visible), do NOT add it, and instead just document the behaviour in the CHANGELOG entry and a code comment, and tell me; (3) a genuinely malformed DO *wrapper* (unterminated dollar quote etc.) must still surface as E_PARSE_ERROR — update `TestPostgresDoMalformedWrapperStillFails` only as far as the decision requires (broken DDL inside a well-formed DO body no longer errors; a broken wrapper still does), and add tests for: rejected DDL in a DO body → clean parse and no phantom symbols; mixed good/bad DO blocks; the two realistic rejected constructs above. (4) Watch the cost: do not re-parse the whole file more than once extra in the common (no rejection) case.
Same rules as before: commit only on review-fix/391, no push, no GitHub posts; end commit messages with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>`. Verify with `go build ./... && go vet ./internal/sem/ && go test -timeout 60m ./internal/sem/...` (ignore the known TestGraphVerbsCoverEveryCommand failure in internal/cli; no need to rerun internal/cli unless you touched it). Report: what you implemented, commit hashes, exact test commands and real results, and anything left open.

input.summary: 389: narrow degraded coverage for config formats
input.message:
Follow-up on PR #389 (branch review-fix/389, your worktree): the maintainer finds it misleading that, after your fix 8eb94aff, ANY unparseable/oversized YAML (e.g. pnpm-lock.yaml, a CI workflow) reports `Coverage: degraded`. Narrow it with a per-file policy, as ONE separate commit on top (so it can be dropped if the maintainer dislikes it).
Intended rule: a partial failure degrades coverage only when the failed file could plausibly have carried graph facts. For programming languages: unchanged (always). For semantic-tier config/data formats (YAML, HCL, CUE, JSON, …): first find out, from the extractors themselves, which files of that format actually produce symbols/relations (e.g. compose files, Kubernetes manifests, Terraform .tf, OpenAPI — whatever the code really recognises, by path pattern or content sniff) — that recognition logic is the single source of truth; reuse or expose it rather than writing a second list. Then: (a) a failure on a file the extractor would recognise as fact-bearing → degraded; (b) a failure on a file of that format with no recognised kind (lockfiles, CI workflows, arbitrary config), or an intentional skip code such as E_MINIFIED / E_FILE_TOO_LARGE on a lockfile/generated file → notice, still listed and counted in the diagnostics so nothing is hidden; (c) when recognition needs content that could not be read/parsed and the path gives no signal, pick the conservative side ONLY for formats where every file is fact-bearing by nature (e.g. HCL .tf) and the notice side for generic containers (YAML/JSON) — and state this rule in the code comment and docs. If the extractors have no usable per-file recognition at all (every YAML file is parsed into generic facts), do not invent heuristics: report back what facts a generic YAML file actually yields and propose the smallest alternative instead of committing.
Keep `effect_scope` values and the schema untouched (this only changes the degraded/notice decision); update the tests you added in 8eb94aff accordingly (HCL .tf parse error → degraded; compose/k8s YAML parse error → degraded; pnpm-lock.yaml too large and a .github/workflows YAML parse error → notice), plus docs/CHANGELOG wording.
Same rules as before: commit only on review-fix/389, no push, no GitHub posts; end the commit message with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>`. Verify with `go build ./... && go vet ./... && go test -timeout 60m ./internal/sem/...` and the internal/cli tests that cover the coverage line (ignore the known TestGraphVerbsCoverEveryCommand failure). Report: what the extractors actually recognise, the rule you implemented, commit hash, exact test commands and real results, anything left open.

input.summary: 389: narrow degraded coverage for config formats
input.message:
Follow-up on PR #389 (branch review-fix/389, your worktree): the maintainer finds it misleading that, after your fix 8eb94aff, ANY unparseable/oversized YAML (e.g. pnpm-lock.yaml, a CI workflow) reports `Coverage: degraded`. Narrow it with a per-file policy, as ONE separate commit on top (so it can be dropped if the maintainer dislikes it).
Intended rule: a partial failure degrades coverage only when the failed file could plausibly have carried graph facts. For programming languages: unchanged (always). For semantic-tier config/data formats (YAML, HCL, CUE, JSON, …): first find out, from the extractors themselves, which files of that format actually produce symbols/relations (e.g. compose files, Kubernetes manifests, Terraform .tf, OpenAPI — whatever the code really recognises, by path pattern or content sniff) — that recognition logic is the single source of truth; reuse or expose it rather than writing a second list. Then: (a) a failure on a file the extractor would recognise as fact-bearing → degraded; (b) a failure on a file of that format with no recognised kind (lockfiles, CI workflows, arbitrary config), or an intentional skip code such as E_MINIFIED / E_FILE_TOO_LARGE on a lockfile/generated file → notice, still listed and counted in the diagnostics so nothing is hidden; (c) when recognition needs content that could not be read/parsed and the path gives no signal, pick the conservative side ONLY for formats where every file is fact-bearing by nature (e.g. HCL .tf) and the notice side for generic containers (YAML/JSON) — and state this rule in the code comment and docs. If the extractors have no usable per-file recognition at all (every YAML file is parsed into generic facts), do not invent heuristics: report back what facts a generic YAML file actually yields and propose the smallest alternative instead of committing.
Keep `effect_scope` values and the schema untouched (this only changes the degraded/notice decision); update the tests you added in 8eb94aff accordingly (HCL .tf parse error → degraded; compose/k8s YAML parse error → degraded; pnpm-lock.yaml too large and a .github/workflows YAML parse error → notice), plus docs/CHANGELOG wording.
Same rules as before: commit only on review-fix/389, no push, no GitHub posts; end the commit message with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>`. Verify with `go build ./... && go vet ./... && go test -timeout 60m ./internal/sem/...` and the internal/cli tests that cover the coverage line (ignore the known TestGraphVerbsCoverEveryCommand failure). Report: what the extractors actually recognise, the rule you implemented, commit hash, exact test commands and real results, anything left open.

input.command:
gh pr create --base main --head fix/gradle-verify-boundary --title "fix(sem): do not derive Gradle VERIFY commands across an unowned project boundary" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Problem

#261 fixed the headline bug from #219, but three Gradle behaviours raised in #249 were still wrong on `main`. Each was reproduced with a failing test before the fix:

- **Undeclared child project climbed to an ancestor build.** With `include ':app'` in the root settings script and an undeclared `lib/` that has its own build script, the narrow tier emitted `./gradlew :test --tests 'ATest'` and the suite tier emitted `./gradlew test` at the root. The suite command can pass without ever testing `lib`.
- **Renamed projects kept their directory path.** `project(':lib').name = 'x'` (and the `setName`, block and Kotlin spellings) still emitted `:lib:test`.
- **Intermediate build roots got no command.** A settings script between the wrapper and the project (`modules/settings.gradle` including `:core`) produced nothing, or a wrong root-level command.

## Fix

All in `internal/sem/search_verify.go`:

- One ownership check now serves both tiers. It recognises a settings script between the wrapper and the project and emits `./gradlew -p modules :core:test`.
- A Gradle derivation declines when an unowned `build.gradle(.kts)` directory lies between the subject and the build being asked. The check lives in the Gradle derivations, not the shared walk, so Maven and Node builds above are still consulted.
- Derivation declines when the settings script renames the project, or renames or relocates one of its ancestors.

Everything fails closed: no command rather than a wrong one. Project names and paths still go through the existing shell-quoting helpers.

## Behaviour change

Repositories whose settings script computes its includes now get no Gradle command for files in subproject directories; they previously got the root `./gradlew test`. This is noted in the CHANGELOG.

## Not included

- The narrow tier still requires the wrapper at the repository root.
- A directory with a settings script but no build script is not treated as a boundary.

## Verification

Run locally: `go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/sem/`, and `go test ./internal/sem/ -run SearchVerify` pass. The full `go test ./internal/sem/...` passed before a final fixture-only tidy of the new test file and was not rerun afterwards; `internal/cli` was not run. CI on this branch will also show the unrelated `TestGraphVerbsCoverEveryCommand` failure until #400 merges.

Test cases adapted from #249; this supersedes that PR.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -1

content.text:
Delivery so far, while four agents keep working (#399, #398, and the #391 and #389 follow-ups):

**Pushed and opened**

- **#400** — the `main` fix (`risk` in `graphVerbs`), new PR.
- **#401** — the Gradle boundary fix, new PR that supersedes #249.
- **#390** — regenerated `NOTICES` pushed to the Dependabot branch.
- **#152** and **#146** — the RFD refreshes pushed to their branches (each includes a merge of `main`).

**Blocked: the two fork PRs, #397 and #392.** Both allow maintainer edits, and I read through the reworked #397 pruning code before trying, but the permission classifier denied pushing to contributors' forks. I haven't worked around it. If you want them delivered that way, you can run the pushes yourself:

```
! git push https://github.com/garvit-arora/entire-graph.git review-fix/397:fix/prune-stale-cache-versions
! git push https://github.com/Beehtrix/entire-graph.git review-fix/392:fix-guide-remember-path-rule-588
```

Both are fast-forwards on top of the contributors' commits. The same block will probably apply to #399 and #398 once their fixes are ready, since those are fork branches too.

**On your question 3 (misleading "degraded"):** my suggestion is a per-file rule, which the #389 agent is now implementing as one separate commit you can drop:

- A failure in a programming language always degrades coverage, as before.
- A failure in a config format degrades coverage only when the file is a kind the extractor produces facts from, such as a compose file, a Kubernetes manifest or Terraform.
- Lockfiles, CI workflows and other config with no recognised kind become a notice, still listed and counted.

The recognition comes from the extractors themselves, not a second list. If the extractors turn out to have no per-file recognition, the agent will report back instead of inventing heuristics.

**Still pending:** #391 and #389 get pushed once their follow-up commits and tests are done. Both #400 and #401 will show the `graphVerbs` failure pattern until #400 merges — #400 itself should go green.

**What the fallback does**

- When DDL projected out of a PL/pgSQL DO body is rejected by the grammar, that one block is masked whole, as on `main`. Other DO blocks in the same file keep their projected DDL.
- There is no whole-file re-parse. The extra cost is one small parse per DO block that contains DDL.
- A genuinely malformed DO wrapper, such as an unterminated dollar quote, still gives a parse error.

`internal/sem` passes at the final commit (651s). `internal/cli` was not rerun after the fallback; it wasn't touched, and its earlier run failed only on the known `graphVerbs` test.

- **The fallback is silent.** No existing warning mechanism fits, and a real warning would need a new schema-visible diagnostic code, so the agent did not add one. A masked block's declarations are simply not indexed, with no diagnostic. This is documented in the CHANGELOG entry and a code comment. Adding a warning code is a schema decision for you.
- **It is all-or-nothing per block.** One rejected statement drops that block's valid sibling declarations too. That matches `main`'s behaviour; a per-statement fallback is possible if you want it.

All agent work is finished. #389 now uses the existing 5% health rule and is pushed, and the `main` fix (#400) is green on all 35 CI checks; its only failing check is "Entire Gates", which on the other PRs was the missing approval.

## #389: coverage follows the health status

The agent `Coverage:` line now prints `degraded` or `unsafe` only when the health status says so, and `notice` otherwise. The PR's parallel rule was removed as dead code; `effect_scope` and schema 1.6 are untouched. In the tests, 1 flagged file of 25 gives `notice` and 1 of 20 gives `degraded`. `internal/sem` passes; `internal/cli` fails only on the known `graphVerbs` test.

Two things in it are yours to confirm:

- **One deviation from "exactly health".** A failure that affects the whole snapshot (a repo-ignore shortfall, a spent analysis budget) still gives `degraded` on its own, because health has no per-file numerator for those. Removing that is a three-line change.
- **The Terraform gap is real, and this change exposes it.** A test with 5 `.tf` files, 4 of them broken, gives `source_files: 0` and status `ok`, so such a repo now prints `Coverage: notice`. The fix would be to count semantic-tier config languages (HCL, YAML, CUE) as source in health. The catch is that every YAML file, lockfiles and CI config included, then enlarges the denominator, and the published `health` numbers change. I'd count HCL and CUE but leave YAML out; say if you want that.

The agent also found and fixed a spot the PR had missed: the tiny-budget fallback marker still used "any partial failure means degraded".

## Where everything stands

| PR | State |
|---|---|
| #400 `main` fix | Open, CI green, needs approval and merge |
| #401 Gradle boundary fix | Open, supersedes #249 |
| #391 Postgres | Fixes pushed, including the DO-block fallback |
| #389 `effect_scope` | Fixes pushed, now on schema 1.6 and the 5% rule |
| #390 Dependabot | `NOTICES` pushed |
| #152, #146 RFDs | Refreshes pushed |
| #399, #398, #397, #392 | Fixed locally on `review-fix/<N>`, not pushed |

The four unpushed ones are fork branches, and the permission classifier blocked me from pushing to contributors' forks. All four allow maintainer edits and are fast-forwards, so you can push them yourself:

```
! git push https://github.com/rodbegbie/entire-graph.git review-fix/399:feature/rust-grammar-v0.24.2
! git push https://github.com/rodbegbie/entire-graph.git review-fix/398:feature/grammar-refresh-fsharp-patch
! git push https://github.com/garvit-arora/entire-graph.git review-fix/397:fix/prune-stale-cache-versions
! git push https://github.com/Beehtrix/entire-graph.git review-fix/392:fix-guide-remember-path-rule-588
```

## Caveats on what was pushed

- I read the reworked #397 pruning code myself, but not the other diffs; the rest rests on the agents' reports and test runs.
- I posted no comments, so the pushes to the #389 and #146 branches (not your branches) arrive unexplained beyond their commit messages.
- Every pushed PR will show the `graphVerbs` test failure until #400 merges.
- The #391 fallback is silent: a masked DO block produces no diagnostic, because a warning would need a new schema-visible code.

## Suggested merge order

1. #400.
2. #391, squash-merged; it keeps revision 8.
3. #399, which takes revision 9 and will need a trivial conflict fix after #391.
4. The rest in any order, with #392 held until entire-brain#605 is ready.

Not touched: #237, #232, #388, #300, #386. #249 can be closed once #401 lands.

content.text:
#397 is retitled to "fix(sem): prune older, idle cache version directories".

There are two open points on #389, both about when `entire graph query --format agent` prints `Coverage: degraded` instead of `Coverage: notice`.

## 1. Whole-snapshot failures still degrade on their own

You asked for the `Coverage:` level to follow the existing 5% health rule. The agent kept one exception: a failure that applies to the whole snapshot, not to one file, still prints `degraded` by itself. The two cases are a repo-ignore shortfall and a spent analysis budget.

The reason is that the health rule counts flagged source files, and these failures have no file to count. Without the exception, a query over a corpus that was silently narrowed would print `notice`.

- **Keep the exception (my recommendation):** these are the cases where the answer may be missing code without any per-file signal.
- **Remove it:** the line then follows health exactly; it is a three-line removal.

## 2. Terraform and other config languages are invisible to the health rule

The health rule only counts "source" files, and HCL, YAML and CUE are classed as non-source. The agent tested this: with 5 `.tf` files, 4 of them failing to parse, health reports zero source files and status `ok`. So a mostly broken Terraform repo now prints `Coverage: notice`, even though the graph does extract resources and relations from those files.

The fix is to count config languages the graph extracts facts from as source in health. The cost is that published health numbers change (`source_files`, `flagged_files`, per-language entries, and the status for affected repos).

- **Count HCL and CUE, leave YAML out (my recommendation):** almost every HCL and CUE file carries facts, so they belong in the count. YAML is mostly lockfiles and CI config, which would inflate the denominator and make the 5% threshold harder to reach for real code failures.
- **Count all three:** consistent with the capabilities registry, but with the YAML dilution above.
- **Leave as is:** Terraform-heavy repos keep under-reporting failures.

One caveat on my recommendation: leaving YAML out means a repo of broken Kubernetes or compose manifests still reads `ok`. Fixing that properly needs a per-file notion of which YAML files carry facts, which is the approach we dropped earlier.

Tell me which way to go on each and I'll have the changes made on the #389 branch.

content.text:
On reflection, my case for excluding YAML was weak, and I'd now count all three.

My argument was dilution: most YAML files are lockfiles and CI config, so adding them to the denominator makes the 5% threshold harder to reach for real code failures. I hadn't measured that. In this repo it's negligible: 13 YAML files out of about 1,200 tracked, against 846 Go files. That is one repo, so it doesn't settle the question for a Kubernetes-heavy one, but there YAML is the code and should count.

Two other things undercut the exclusion:

- **The lockfile case is already handled.** What originally bothered you was an oversized `pnpm-lock.yaml` causing "degraded". The health rule already treats `E_FILE_TOO_LARGE` and `E_MINIFIED` as intentional skips that don't count as flagged, so that file wouldn't degrade coverage even with YAML counted.
- **Excluding YAML leaves the same hole I was fixing for Terraform.** A repo of broken Kubernetes or compose manifests would still read `ok`.

Counting all three also gives one rule with no special case: a language is source for health if the capabilities registry says the graph extracts facts from it.

The remaining cost is the same either way: published health numbers change (`source_files`, `flagged_files`, per-language entries, and status for affected repos). And one YAML-specific effect stays: a genuinely unparseable CI workflow file counts as one flagged file, which only matters in a repo small enough for one file to reach 5%.

So my recommendation is now: count HCL, YAML and CUE as source in health, driven by the registry. Say the word and I'll have it implemented on the #389 branch as a separate commit.

lastPrompt: Ok, but then the question becomes, which file types are excluded?

content.text:
After the change, 38 formats would stay excluded from health, and all of them are ones the graph extracts no facts from. I checked the current exclusion list in `sourceFileLanguage` against `entire graph capabilities` from the installed binary (v0.6.0): it has 41 entries, and only YAML, HCL and CUE are semantic-tier.

The 38 that stay excluded:

| Group | Formats |
|---|---|
| Documentation | Markdown, reStructuredText, Textile, TeX, BibTeX, Mermaid, VuePress |
| Diffs | Diff, Patch |
| Data | JSON, JSON5, TOML, XML, INI, RON, Property List |
| Infrastructure config | Kustomize, Dockerfile, Bicep, Dhall, Nix, Puppet, Augeas |
| Build files | Make, CMake, Cabal, MSBuild Project, Just, Rake |
| Tool and package config | Babel Config, EditorConfig, Dotenv, Git Ignore, NPM Config, Homebrew Bundle, Bundler, Pip Requirements, RubyGems |

Files with no recognised language are also not counted, as today.

So the resulting rule is easy to state: a file counts toward health unless it is a documentation, data or config format that the graph only inventories.

The list is not the same as "inventory-only". There are 149 inventory-only languages in the registry, and only these 38 are excluded. The other 111 or so are programming, template and stylesheet languages the graph doesn't parse semantically, and they deliberately count as source so that a repo mostly in an unsupported language reads as badly covered.

Two entries are judgment calls you may want to revisit, though I'd leave them for now:

- **Kustomize, Bicep, Nix, Puppet, Dockerfile:** these are infrastructure code in the same spirit as HCL. They are excluded only because the graph extracts nothing from them today. If one becomes semantic-tier, a registry-driven rule moves it into health automatically.
- **JSON:** excluded, so a failure in a JSON file never affects the level. That matches today's behaviour.

Shall I have the registry-driven version implemented on the #389 branch as a separate commit?

message.content: So a failure in a Dockerfile always downgrades to degraded?

content.text:
No, the opposite: a failure in a Dockerfile never affects the level. Dockerfile is on the excluded list, so it counts neither as a source file nor as a flagged file, and the health status ignores it.

"Excluded" in that table meant excluded from the health calculation, not excluded from the graph. The failure is still listed and counted in the diagnostics; it just can't move the level from `notice` to `degraded`.

In practice a Dockerfile rarely produces a failure at all. It is inventory-only, so the graph records the file without parsing it, and the only failures it could raise are things like a read error or an oversized file.

The same holds for the other 37 excluded formats. After the change, the only formats whose failures would newly count are YAML, HCL and CUE, and even then a failure only causes `degraded` once flagged files reach 5% of counted source files.

content.text:
It was a side effect of an earlier fix in this session, not something YAML-specific, and it no longer exists on the #389 branch. The sequence was:

1. **On `main`:** the agent `Coverage:` line prints `degraded` whenever there is any partial failure at all, in any file type. This repo shows it today: 7 failures in about 1,070 files, one of them a minified JSON file under `.entire/runners/`, and the line reads "degraded".

2. **#389 as its author wrote it:** it narrowed that to "any failure that can affect code", and exempted config and data formats, YAML included. At that point a YAML failure gave `notice`.

3. **The first fix pass:** the reviewer pointed out that YAML and HCL are formats the graph does extract facts from (compose files, Kubernetes manifests, Terraform), so exempting them hides real gaps. The fix agent removed the exemption for those formats. The side effect was that any failing YAML file, a lockfile or a CI workflow included, now gave `degraded`. I reported that to you as a caveat, and that is what you called misleading.

4. **The second fix, after you pointed to the 5% rule:** the whole "any failure" logic was replaced. The line now follows the existing health status, which needs flagged files to reach 5% of source files and does not count YAML at all.

So in the version now pushed to #389, a YAML failure never causes `degraded`. That fixed your complaint but swung too far the other way: a Terraform or Kubernetes repo full of broken files reads fine.

The change I'm proposing sits in between: count YAML, HCL and CUE as source files, so their failures matter, but only once flagged files reach the 5% threshold. One broken CI workflow in a normal repo would still read `notice`.

[]
## Summary

Three commits. Warnings that cannot affect code facts stop carrying weight, and the verdict is published in a form machines can read.

**1. `fix(cli)`: "Coverage: degraded" only for failures that can reach code.** The agent coverage line said `degraded` (compact `!D`) whenever a search response had any partial failure. On entire-brain every query opened with `Coverage: degraded` because of 47 JSON partial failures: 46 `E_MINIFIED` benchmark fixtures and one `E_FILE_TOO_LARGE` 16.8 MB snapshot. Every Go and Python file had parsed. The level is now `degraded` only for a failure that is not confined to one file (repo-ignore shortfalls, a spent budget) or that is confined to a source file. File-confined failures in data, config and documentation formats give `notice`. They are still counted and listed exactly as before, and repo-ignore hoisting is unchanged. The format policy reuses `sourceFileLanguage` (`internal/sem/health.go`), the classification `completeness.health` already uses, so the coverage line and health agree on which files are source. A file whose language cannot be resolved counts as source.

**2. `fix(sem)`: valid Go the grammar cannot parse is `W_GO_GRAMMAR_GAP`, not `E_PARSE_ERROR`.** Go 1.26 accepts `new(expr)` (`new(0)`, `new("4242")`, `new(now.Add(d))`). The bundled smacker grammar and upstream tree-sitter-go master both still require a type there, so a dependency bump would not fix it. Four gofmt-clean entiredb test files were reported as `E_PARSE_ERROR`, which fed `degraded`, although their definitions and outer calls survive the recovery. When the tree-sitter parse of a Go file has errors, `ParseWithStatusCtx` now asks `go/parser` (`SkipObjectResolution`). If it accepts the bytes, the status gets `GrammarGap` and code `W_GO_GRAMMAR_GAP`. That status is the one chokepoint every consumer converts:
- snapshot and search report a warning naming the file instead of a partial failure, so Go health stops counting it;
- `diff` and the diff dependents scan keep their existing kept/suppressed handling with the new code and an honest effect.

The effect says the file is valid Go the bundled grammar cannot fully parse, and that facts inside that construct may be missing. It names no remedy, because none is needed. Go that `go/parser` rejects keeps `E_PARSE_ERROR`. Records cache v25 and search cache v30 retire the old entries.

**3. `feat(sem)`: machine-readable `effect_scope` (schema 1.5).** Every warning and partial failure carries `effect_scope`, including `diff`/`commit`/`checkpoint` warnings:
- `file`: the loss is confined to `file_path` (its symbols, and relations that start or end at them);
- `snapshot`: no file bound.

It is `DiagnosticEffectScope(code, file_path)`, stamped where diagnostics leave the provider: snapshot summary, derived selective view, search response, diff result. A source-scanning test fails on any code literal that is unclassified or stale. Capabilities advertise `optional_local_only_features.partial_failure_effect_scope: true`, and `schema_features` lists it too.

## Design decisions

- **Language table:** the existing `sourceFileLanguage` health policy. No second list.
- **Cache strategy:** bump, not derive-at-serialization. `ProviderWarning` is reachable from the persisted `Result`, whose ADR 0001 guard forbids JSON hooks. Commit 2 bumps `providerRecordsCacheVersion` v24→v25 and `searchSnapshotCacheVersion` v29→v30. Commit 3's schema bump re-keys both cache families: `TestCacheKeysAddressTheSchemaVersion`, `TestProviderRecordsCacheMissesEntryFromAnotherSchemaVersion` and `TestSearchSnapshotCacheMissesPersistedEntryFromAnotherSchemaVersion` already pin that. Live check: a cache dir written by the base build (same `dev` provider version) is a miss for the new build (`Index: cache-miss`), then a hit on the next run, and the warm JSON carries `effect_scope`.
- **Schema:** additive optional field, so `SchemaVersion` 1.4→1.5 per ADR 0001. The `Result` shape is re-pinned with its new digest, and the ADR has a 1.5 section. `IdentityRevision` is unchanged ("5").

## Measurements

The go/parser check runs only for Go files whose tree-sitter parse already errored. Below: cold `index --head` on entiredb (2,608 files, 1,984 Go), with base = origin/main 28382d8e and new = this branch. Runs were interleaved base/new, each with a fresh `--cache-dir`, under the shared measure lock. A brain `workspace watch --distill` daemon was using about 1.1 cores the whole time, and both arms saw it.

| repo | command | base (s) | new (s) | base median | new median | load1 before / after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| entiredb | `index --head` (cold) | 6.51, 6.33, 6.38 | 6.41, 6.32, 6.35 | **6.38** | **6.35** | 7.57 / 6.98 |

There is no measurable cost.

**Output identity.** I compared the `snapshot --format ndjson` streams from base and new after `g2-strip.py` normalization:

| repo | data records | identical | header and summary differences |
|---|---|---|---|
| entiredb | 238,985 | yes | `schema_version` 1.4→1.5, plus the new `schema_features` entry. Four Go files moved from `E_PARSE_ERROR` partial failures to `W_GO_GRAMMAR_GAP` warnings, so partial failures went 15→11 and warnings 1→5. Go `health.flagged_files` went 4→0, and `effect_scope` appears on every diagnostic. |
| entire-brain | 235,898 | yes | schema and `schema_features`, plus `effect_scope` on all 47 failures and the 1 warning |

**Live checks (built binaries, not the installed one):**
1. entire-brain: `query --head --format agent` now prints `Coverage: notice (15 languages/1783 files; 0 warnings; 47 partial failures)` and still lists the JSON partials. Base prints `degraded`, and that is the only line of the payload that differs.
2. entiredb: the four `new(expr)` test files (`buildkite_watch_test.go`, `githubperms/service_test.go`, `identity/github_email_identities_test.go`, `regional/author_lookup_test.go`) carry `W_GO_GRAMMAR_GAP` (`effect_scope: file`) and no `E_PARSE_ERROR`. Its SQL, proto and shell parse errors are unchanged.
3. A repo with a real Go syntax error still reports `E_PARSE_ERROR` and `Coverage: degraded`.
4. `capabilities --json` reports `schema_version: 1.5` and `partial_failure_effect_scope: true`.
5. `diff --json` on an entiredb range carries `effect_scope` on every warning, for example `W_UNSUPPORTED_FILE` → `file` and `W_MOVE_AMBIGUOUS` → `snapshot`.

## Test plan

New tests:
- `TestDiagnosticEffectScope` and `TestPartialFailureAffectsCode` (sem table tests).
- `TestAgentCoverageLevelIgnoresDataFormatFailures` (cli).
- `TestParseStatusDefersGoGrammarGapToGoParser`.
- `TestSnapshotReportsGoGrammarGapAsWarning`: snapshot path, health, CALLS survival, and selective-view parity for cold vs derived.
- `TestDiffReportsGoGrammarGapAsWarning`: diff and dependents-scan paths, plus invalid Go.
- `TestGoGrammarGapStaysVisible`: query JSON, query agent output, neighbors agent output.
- `TestEveryDiagnosticCodeHasAnEffectScope`: scans the source; fails on an unclassified or stale code.
- `TestEffectScopeStampNeverMutatesItsInput`.
- `TestEffectScopeOnEveryDiagnostic`: JSON from snapshot, index, query, neighbors and diff, plus the capabilities key.

Updated tests:
- the goldens, regenerated (only schema and effect_scope changes);
- the `Result` shape digest, re-pinned at 1.5;
- the schema-version assertions.

Each guard was weakened and the matching test went red. Every mutation was restored from a byte copy and checked with `cmp`.
- Data-language exemption removed (`PartialFailureAffectsCode` always true): 7 sem cases fail ("minified JSON fixture ... = true, want false").
- Scope check removed: the "snapshot scope beats a data-format path" case fails, in sem and in the cli level test.
- cli level reverted to `len(PartialFailures) > 0`: "want Coverage: notice".
- go/parser deferral disabled: all four grammar-gap tests fail ("valid Go still reported as a partial failure").
- go/parser always accepting: invalid Go becomes a gap and fails ("invalid Go ... want E_PARSE_ERROR").
- Selective view drops the gap warning, or ignores `allowedFiles`: cold/derived parity fails.
- Gap routed back into partial failures: the snapshot test fails.
- Exhaustiveness, three ways: removing a table entry (`W_MOVE_AMBIGUOUS`), adding a code literal to production source (`E_BRAND_NEW_FAILURE`), and adding a stale table entry (`W_RETIRED_CODE`) each fail.
- Diff result left unstamped, or snapshot summary left unstamped: `TestEffectScopeOnEveryDiagnostic` fails.

Local runs:
- `go test -p 1 ./internal/sem` passes (251 s), and so does `./internal/cli` (255 s).
- The focused tests above, plus the stream, pipeline, preindex and warm tests, pass under `-race` with no `DATA RACE`.

content.text:
The author wanted `Coverage: degraded` to mean "a failure that could actually hide code from this answer", with no percentage threshold. I read the PR description to answer this.

**The motivating case.** In entire-brain every query opened with `Coverage: degraded` because of 47 JSON failures: 46 minified benchmark fixtures and one oversized 16.8 MB snapshot. Every Go and Python file had parsed, so the warning was noise.

**The author's rule.**

- `degraded` if a failure is not confined to one file (a repo-ignore shortfall, a spent budget), or is confined to a source file.
- `notice` if the failure is confined to a data, config or documentation file. It is still listed and counted.
- "Source" was decided by the existing health classification, on purpose, so the coverage line and health agree on which files are source. That is how YAML and HCL ended up exempt.

The PR had two other parts, both still in place: the Go grammar-gap downgrade (valid Go 1.26 `new(expr)` that tree-sitter can't parse) and the machine-readable `effect_scope` field.

**Where the pushed version now differs from the author's intent.** The author's rule had no threshold: one real syntax error in one Go file gave `degraded`, and the PR lists that as a live check. Under the 5% rule now on the branch, a single broken Go file in a large repo reads `notice`. I should have flagged that when I redirected the agent to the health rule; it is a real change in behaviour, not just a refactor.

Both rules fix the entire-brain noise, since minified and oversized files don't count under either. They differ on small numbers of real source failures:

| Case | Author's rule | 5% rule (pushed now) |
|---|---|---|
| 47 minified/oversized JSON files | notice | notice |
| 1 broken Go file in 2,000 | degraded | notice |
| 4 of 5 `.tf` files broken | notice | notice (degraded once HCL counts as source) |
| Repo-ignore shortfall or spent budget | degraded | degraded (the exception you kept) |

Decision for you: the author's rule is stricter and arguably more honest for an agent, since the one broken file may be exactly the one the query is about. The 5% rule is quieter and consistent with `health`. I can keep the 5% rule as pushed, or restore the author's "any source-file failure degrades" rule and add HCL, YAML and CUE to what counts as source — that second option is the smallest change from what the author intended. Which do you want?

Maintainer decision on PR #389 (branch review-fix/389 in your worktree; note it has since been PUSHED to origin as fix/partial-failure-effect-scope at 27e26fb0, so only ADD commits — no reset, no amend, no force): restore the PR author's original rule for the agent `Coverage:` level, replacing the health-status rule from 27e26fb0.
The author's rule, exactly as in the PR at 91191330: `degraded` when a partial failure is not confined to one file (effect_scope snapshot: repo-ignore shortfall, spent budget) or is confined to a SOURCE file; `notice` when every failure is confined to a data/config/documentation file; failures still listed and counted. "Source" is decided by the existing `sourceFileLanguage` health policy (so YAML, HCL, CUE, JSON etc. stay exempt, as the author had it — do NOT add the semantic-tier widening from 8eb94aff back: without a threshold it makes any failing YAML lockfile or CI workflow print degraded, which the maintainer rejected). A file whose language cannot be resolved counts as source. No percentage threshold: one real Go syntax error → degraded. Two-state label again (no `Coverage: unsafe`).

content.text:
It is one word in the first lines of output from `entire graph query --format agent`, and its reader is the coding agent, not you. You'd only see it by expanding a tool call in a transcript.

It looks like this, from a query I ran earlier in this session:

```
Coverage: degraded (49 languages/1069 files, 25 excluded by repo ignore rules; 2 warnings; 7 partial failures)
- warning W_REPO_IGNORED_SOURCE: internal/sem/grammars/clojure/parser.c
- partial E_MINIFIED: .entire/runners/trail-review.json
- ... 6 more diagnostics in JSON output
```

- **`degraded`** tells the agent: some files could not be analysed, so this answer may be missing code; check before trusting an empty result.
- **`notice`** tells the agent: there are diagnostics, listed below, but none that should change how much it trusts the answer.

When the output budget is very tight, the same signal is compressed to a short marker (`!D`).

So the whole #389 debate is about how often an agent is told to distrust its results. Too eager, and every query opens with a warning the agent learns to ignore, which was the author's complaint about entire-brain. Too quiet, and the agent trusts an answer that is missing the one broken file it asked about.

What a human sees is a separate mechanism. The `--format text` output has its own `Completeness:` block, and `entire graph health` reports the status directly. From the code I read, both of those are driven by the health status with the 5% threshold, and #389 does not change that rule. So restoring the author's rule affects only the agent-facing line; the human-facing reports stay on the 5% rule.

Merge #400 first, then the three PRs that rewrite the golden fixtures one at a time, then the independent ones.

| # | PR | Why here | Before merging |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | #400 `main` fix | Unblocks CI for everything else | Approve it; its only failing check is "Entire Gates" (approval) |
| 2 | #391 Postgres | Keeps `IdentityRevision` 8; other PRs are numbered around it | Update from `main`; squash-merge |
| 3 | #389 `effect_scope` | Takes schema 1.6; touches the same golden header lines as #391 | Update from `main`, regenerate goldens; squash-merge |
| 4 | #399 Rust grammar | Takes revision 9, so it must follow #391 | Approve the CI run; fix the trivial `provider.go` comment and golden conflicts |
| 5 | #398 F# patch | Independent; same manifest file as #399 but different entries | Approve the CI run; ideally the author confirms the real refresh gives an empty diff |
| 6 | #397 cache prune | Independent | Approve the CI run |
| 7 | #401 Gradle fix | Independent | Then close #249 as superseded |
| 8 | #390 Dependabot Go modules | Independent | Update from `main` |
| 9 | #386 Dependabot `setup-python` | Independent | Comment `@dependabot rebase` after #400 |
| 10 | #392 guide text | Must land together with entire-brain#605 | Hold until #605 is ready |

Things that apply across the list:

- **Goldens conflict in sequence.** #391, #389 and #399 each change the header line of the same 29 golden files, so each one needs its goldens regenerated after the previous one merges. That is why they go one at a time.

66:<<<<<<< HEAD

- Valid Go that the bundled tree-sitter grammar cannot fully parse (Go 1.26's
  `new(expr)`, for example `new(0)`) is no longer reported as an `E_PARSE_ERROR`
  partial failure. When `go/parser` accepts the file, snapshots, search and
  `diff` report a `W_GO_GRAMMAR_GAP` warning naming it instead: it does not
  count against completeness, and its effect says facts inside the construct the
  grammar could not parse may be missing. The downgrade applies only while the
  recovered tree still yields every top-level function, method and type
  `go/parser` finds: a valid file whose recovery lost a declaration keeps its
  counted `E_PARSE_ERROR` partial failure, with the lost names in `detail`. Go
  that `go/parser` rejects keeps `E_PARSE_ERROR`. Records and search caches are versioned so a cached

content.text:
They already run in parallel; the delay is one job, `test (macos-latest)`, and that one can be split.

I looked at the latest runs of `test.yml`. Every job starts within a few seconds of the trigger, and almost everything is done in about 9 minutes:

| Job | Time |
|---|---|
| Lint, build, notices, small gates | under 3 min each |
| `test (ubuntu-latest)` | about 5 min |
| Windows (compile, 8 shards, verify) | done about 9 min after trigger |
| `test (macos-latest)` | 17.5 min on the last `main` run; over 19 min and still running on #389 |

So macOS alone roughly doubles the wait. It runs the whole suite as a single `go test -timeout 30m ./...` on a GitHub-hosted macOS runner, while Ubuntu uses an 8-core Depot runner and Windows is already sharded. The workflow has a comment saying macOS stays GitHub-hosted because of Depot's macOS concurrency cap.

**Recommendation: shard the macOS test job by package.** Nearly all the time is in two packages, `internal/sem` and `internal/cli`, which currently compete for the same few cores. Running them as separate jobs, plus one for everything else, should bring macOS close to the longer of the two. I'd guess 8–10 minutes, but that is an estimate; each shard still has to compile the CGO grammars, and I haven't measured it.

One constraint: `test (macos-latest)` is a required check on `main`. The Windows setup already solves this with a small final job that keeps the old check name and passes only if all shards pass, and the macOS split would copy that pattern.

Two alternatives, both weaker:

- **A larger macOS runner:** a one-line change, but it costs more per minute and still runs everything in one job.
- **Finer shards inside `internal/sem`, like the Windows harness:** faster still, but it means porting the shard planner to macOS. Worth doing only if the package split isn't enough.

Want me to open a PR that splits the macOS job into the three package shards with the aggregate check?

content.text:
Yes, macOS is the only slow part. Here are the times for the latest #389 run, per workflow:

| Workflow | Wall time |
|---|---|
| `test` | 20 min 18 s |
| CodeQL analysis (shown as "PR #389") | 6 min 34 s |
| `lazy-fetch git matrix` | 1 min 14 s |
| `bench-memory-guards` | 16 s |
| `bench-memory-kit` | 14 s |

Inside `test`, the slowest jobs were:

| Job | Time |
|---|---|
| `test (macos-latest)` | 20 min 14 s |
| Windows, end to end (compile, 8 shards, verify) | about 9 min |
| Slowest single Windows shard | 6 min 11 s |
| `test (ubuntu-latest)` | 5 min 7 s |
| Everything else (lint, builds, notices, small gates) | under 3 min each |

So the `test` workflow takes 20 minutes only because of the one macOS job; without it, the workflow would finish in about 9 minutes, and CodeQL at 6.5 minutes would not be the limit either.

"Entire Gates" also showed 20 min 23 s, almost exactly matching the `test` workflow. One of its gates is "Checks", so it appears to wait for CI to finish and is not slow in its own right. That is my reading of the timing, not something I confirmed in its details.

After a macOS split, the next limit would be Windows at about 9 minutes, of which 2.5 minutes is the "compile and plan" step every shard waits on. That makes a realistic floor of roughly 9–10 minutes per PR, down from 20.

content.content:
# Production Windows test sharding

The `test` workflow compiles the configured CGO test binaries once on a
standard ephemeral Windows runner, inventories every default-runnable root
(`Test`, `Example`, and `Fuzz`, but never `Benchmark`), and assigns those roots
to eight deterministic weighted shards. The compiled binaries and immutable
plan are downloaded by eight independent standard Windows runners.

`settings.json` is the only tuning surface. Its defaults preserve `go test`
semantics: shuffle is off, `-parallel` and `GOMAXPROCS` are unset, and every
shard has a 30-minute package timeout. Historical timings only seed known
roots. The inventory produced from the current compiled binary is
authoritative, so a newly added root is always included with the configured
default weight.

Direct test-binary launches preserve the environment and lifecycle details
that `cmd/go` supplies: `PWD` is the absolute package directory, the active
`GOTOOLDIR` is first on `PATH`, and `-test.paniconexit0` is unconditional.
Every shard clears only the Go test-result cache once before execution while
retaining setup-go's module and build caches. Before and after prepare, shard,
and non-heavy execution, the harness requires a clean tracked worktree and an
unchanged commit.

The target identity is fixed to native `windows/amd64` with `CGO_ENABLED=1`
through every inventory, plan, runner record, and verification boundary.
`inventory_testmain.go` parses only the target-selected `TestGoFiles` and
`XTestGoFiles`; settings pin each top-level `TestMain` declaration by filename
and the SHA-256 of its exact AST source range after LF normalization. That
makes lifecycle-hook drift fail closed while remaining stable across LF and
CRLF checkouts.

The verifier has no monolithic reference run. It instead fails closed unless
the plan is a disjoint, complete partition of the compiled inventories; every
planned root has exactly one top-level `run` and one successful terminal
event; each package process starts and terminates with the planned
multiplicity; every non-heavy target-Windows package runs exactly once; all
binary hashes, repository/toolchain identities, metadata exits, and serialized
Windows command-line budgets agree. Exit fields are schema-mandated: prepare's
top-level result and every expected operation, each shard's cache clean and
planned invocation, and the non-heavy clean/test sequence must all be present
and zero.

The workflow keeps native Windows `go build ./...` coverage and adds a separate
Windows `go vet ./...` job. It uses only standard ephemeral hosted runners.
{
  "schema": "entire-graph.windows-ci.settings.v1",
  "shardCount": 8,
  "defaultWeightSeconds": 1.0,
  "timeout": "30m",
  "commandLineLimit": 30000,
  "shuffle": "off",
  "testParallel": null,
  "goMaxProcs": null,
  "heavyPackages": [
    {
      "argument": "./internal/sem",
      "importPath": "github.com/entireio/entire-graph/internal/sem",
      "binaryName": "sem.test.exe",
      "expectedTestMainDeclarations": [
        {
          "file": "provider_gitdir_unc_windows_test.go",
          "normalizedSourceSha256": "cf905cf8cb6b96a67c68fc78718e2919cd4febcf681a3322e8629c296f6776f7"
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "argument": "./internal/cli",
      "importPath": "github.com/entireio/entire-graph/internal/cli",
      "binaryName": "cli.test.exe",
      "expectedTestMainDeclarations": [
        {
          "file": "git_metadata_guard_windows_test.go",
          "normalizedSourceSha256": "40a216486cd8465740ec22fb31b98241c943d5ddfd50097d95967dc388fb559a"
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "argument": "./internal/gitutil",
      "importPath": "github.com/entireio/entire-graph/internal/gitutil",
      "binaryName": "gitutil.test.exe",
      "expectedTestMainDeclarations": []
    }
  ]
}
  windows-test-prepare:
    name: test (windows-latest) / compile and plan
    runs-on: depot-windows-2025-8
    timeout-minutes: 30
    outputs:
      shard-matrix: ${{ steps.shard-matrix.outputs.value }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v7.0.0
        with:
          go-version: "1.27.x"
          cache-dependency-path: go.sum
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7.0.0
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - name: Validate the Windows sharding harness
        run: python -B -m unittest discover -s tools/ci-bench/windows-production/tests -p "test_*.py" -v
      - name: Compile once and inventory default-runnable roots
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
          $repository = (Resolve-Path -LiteralPath '.').Path
          $output = Join-Path $env:RUNNER_TEMP 'windows-test-bundle'
          & python -B tools/ci-bench/windows-production/prepare.py `
            --repository $repository `
            --output $output `
            --settings tools/ci-bench/windows-production/settings.json `
            --weights tools/ci-bench/windows-production/historical-weights.json `
            --expected-repository-sha '${{ github.sha }}'
          if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { exit $LASTEXITCODE }
      - name: Export the authoritative shard matrix
        id: shard-matrix
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
          $planPath = Join-Path $env:RUNNER_TEMP 'windows-test-bundle/plan.json'
          $plan = Get-Content -LiteralPath $planPath -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json
          $indexes = @($plan.shards | ForEach-Object { [int] $_.index })
          if ($indexes.Count -ne [int] $plan.shardCount -or $indexes.Count -eq 0) {
            throw 'plan shard indexes do not match shardCount'
          }
          $matrix = ConvertTo-Json -InputObject $indexes -Compress
          "value=$matrix" | Out-File -LiteralPath $env:GITHUB_OUTPUT -Encoding utf8 -Append
      - name: Upload immutable Windows test bundle
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@cf430e030ddbb5b0abf93d22962f4752f3646cd9 # v7.0.2
        with:
          name: windows-test-bundle
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-bundle
          if-no-files-found: error
          compression-level: 0
          retention-days: 3

  windows-test-shards:
    name: test (windows-latest) / shard ${{ matrix.shard }}
    needs: windows-test-prepare
    runs-on: depot-windows-2025-8
    timeout-minutes: 105
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      max-parallel: 8
      matrix:
        shard: ${{ fromJSON(needs.windows-test-prepare.outputs.shard-matrix) }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v7.0.0
        with:
          go-version: "1.27.x"
          cache-dependency-path: go.sum
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7.0.0
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          name: windows-test-bundle
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-bundle
      - name: Execute the assigned compiled roots
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
          $repository = (Resolve-Path -LiteralPath '.').Path
          $bundle = (Resolve-Path -LiteralPath '${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-bundle').Path
          $output = Join-Path $env:RUNNER_TEMP 'windows-test-shard-${{ matrix.shard }}'
          & python -B tools/ci-bench/windows-production/run_shard.py `
            --repository $repository `
            --bundle $bundle `
            --output $output `
            --shard-index '${{ matrix.shard }}' `
            --expected-repository-sha '${{ github.sha }}'
          exit $LASTEXITCODE
      - name: Upload shard evidence
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@cf430e030ddbb5b0abf93d22962f4752f3646cd9 # v7.0.2
        with:
          name: windows-test-shard-${{ matrix.shard }}
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-shard-${{ matrix.shard }}
          if-no-files-found: error
          retention-days: 3

  windows-test-other:
    name: test (windows-latest) / non-heavy packages
    needs: windows-test-prepare
    runs-on: depot-windows-2025-4
    timeout-minutes: 40
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v7.0.0
        with:
          go-version: "1.27.x"
          cache-dependency-path: go.sum
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7.0.0
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          name: windows-test-bundle
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-bundle
      - name: Run every target-Windows non-heavy package once
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
          $repository = (Resolve-Path -LiteralPath '.').Path
          $bundle = (Resolve-Path -LiteralPath '${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-bundle').Path
          $output = Join-Path $env:RUNNER_TEMP 'windows-test-other'
          & python -B tools/ci-bench/windows-production/run_other.py `
            --repository $repository `
            --bundle $bundle `
            --output $output `
            --expected-repository-sha '${{ github.sha }}'
          exit $LASTEXITCODE
      - name: Upload non-heavy package evidence
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@cf430e030ddbb5b0abf93d22962f4752f3646cd9 # v7.0.2
        with:

# Production Windows test sharding

The `test` workflow compiles the configured CGO test binaries once on a
standard ephemeral Windows runner, inventories every default-runnable root
(`Test`, `Example`, and `Fuzz`, but never `Benchmark`), and assigns those roots
to eight deterministic weighted shards. The compiled binaries and immutable
plan are downloaded by eight independent standard Windows runners.

`settings.json` is the only tuning surface. Its defaults preserve `go test`
semantics: shuffle is off, `-parallel` and `GOMAXPROCS` are unset, and every
shard has a 30-minute package timeout. Historical timings only seed known
roots. The inventory produced from the current compiled binary is
authoritative, so a newly added root is always included with the configured
default weight.

Direct test-binary launches preserve the environment and lifecycle details
that `cmd/go` supplies: `PWD` is the absolute package directory, the active
`GOTOOLDIR` is first on `PATH`, and `-test.paniconexit0` is unconditional.
Every shard clears only the Go test-result cache once before execution while
retaining setup-go's module and build caches. Before and after prepare, shard,
and non-heavy execution, the harness requires a clean tracked worktree and an
unchanged commit.

The target identity is fixed to native `windows/amd64` with `CGO_ENABLED=1`
through every inventory, plan, runner record, and verification boundary.
`inventory_testmain.go` parses only the target-selected `TestGoFiles` and
`XTestGoFiles`; settings pin each top-level `TestMain` declaration by filename
and the SHA-256 of its exact AST source range after LF normalization. That
makes lifecycle-hook drift fail closed while remaining stable across LF and
CRLF checkouts.

The verifier has no monolithic reference run. It instead fails closed unless
the plan is a disjoint, complete partition of the compiled inventories; every
planned root has exactly one top-level `run` and one successful terminal
event; each package process starts and terminates with the planned
multiplicity; every non-heavy target-Windows package runs exactly once; all
binary hashes, repository/toolchain identities, metadata exits, and serialized
Windows command-line budgets agree. Exit fields are schema-mandated: prepare's
top-level result and every expected operation, each shard's cache clean and
planned invocation, and the non-heavy clean/test sequence must all be present
and zero.

The workflow keeps native Windows `go build ./...` coverage and adds a separate
Windows `go vet ./...` job. It uses only standard ephemeral hosted runners.

input.prompt:
Task: port the repository's Windows CI test-sharding harness so the macOS test job is sharded the same way. Repo: entire-graph (Go CLI with CGO tree-sitter grammars; read AGENTS.md at the repo root). Work ONLY in the existing git worktree `/Users/m1/Projects/entire-graph/.claude/worktrees/ci-macos-shards`, on its branch `ci/macos-test-shards` (already created from current origin/main). Commit there; do NOT push, do not open a PR, do not post to GitHub, do not touch other branches or worktrees, do not run `entire session ...` / `entire enable|disable|clean|auth`.

Why: in `.github/workflows/test.yml` every job finishes within ~9 minutes except `test (macos-latest)`, which runs `go test -timeout 30m ./...` as ONE job on the GitHub-hosted `macos-latest` runner (arm64, few cores) and takes 17–20 minutes; it alone doubles CI wall time. Measured on a recent run: test (ubuntu-latest) 5 min; Windows end to end ~9 min (compile-and-plan 2.6 min, then 8 shards of 3.6–6.2 min, non-heavy packages 2.7 min, verify 17 s). Nearly all test time is in two packages, `./internal/sem` and `./internal/cli` (each ~6 min on an M1 when run alone).

What exists (read all of it first): `tools/ci-bench/windows-production/` — README.md, settings.json, historical-weights.json, prepare.py (compile the heavy packages' test binaries once, inventory default-runnable roots, build the plan), plan_shards.py, run_shard.py, run_other.py (non-heavy packages), verify_results.py (fail-closed coverage/integrity verification), inventory_testmain.go, and tests/ (incl. test_workflow_contract.py, which pins the workflow shape). The workflow jobs `windows-test-prepare`, `windows-test-shards`, `windows-test-other`, `windows-test-vet`, `windows-test-verify` and the aggregate `windows-test` (which keeps the required check name `test (windows-latest)`) use it. The harness currently hard-codes the target identity native windows/amd64, `.exe` binary names, a Windows command-line budget, pwsh steps, and per-file TestMain pins for `*_windows_test.go`.

What to build:
1. Generalise the harness to a target parameter so the SAME code serves windows/amd64 (behaviour and outputs unchanged — its existing unit tests must keep passing unmodified except where a test hard-codes something you deliberately parametrise) and darwin/arm64. Prefer the smallest honest generalisation over a copy: per-target settings (keep `settings.json` for Windows as is; add a macOS settings file with its own shardCount, heavy packages, binary names without `.exe`, the correct `expectedTestMainDeclarations` for the files Go selects on darwin, and a command-line limit appropriate for macOS/POSIX — derive it from the real ARG_MAX-style constraint rather than reusing the Windows number, and document it), per-target historical weights (seed macOS weights from a real local run if cheap; otherwise the default weight — say which), and artifact/bundle names per target. Do not rename the directory unless leaving the name would be actively misleading; if you keep it, update the README to say it now serves both targets.
2. Workflow: replace the single macOS leg of the `test` matrix with macOS jobs mirroring the Windows ones — compile-and-plan, shards (matrix from the plan), non-heavy packages, verify, and an aggregate job that keeps the EXACT check name `test (macos-latest)` (it is a required check on main; the comment in the workflow about required-check identity explains the pattern). Ubuntu's `test (ubuntu-latest)` stays a single job with its current name. Use bash steps on macOS (no pwsh). Keep the pinned action versions/SHAs style used in the file. macOS stays on the GitHub-hosted `macos-latest` runner (a workflow comment explains Depot's macOS concurrency cap). IMPORTANT capacity constraint: GitHub-hosted macOS concurrency is limited per account (as low as 5 concurrent macOS jobs on some plans) and this workflow already runs other macOS jobs (build, statusline, prompt-context-hook), so do NOT use 8 macOS shards: default the macOS shardCount to 4 (configurable in the macOS settings file) and put a comment saying why. The verify and aggregate jobs can run on the Ubuntu runner as the Windows ones do. A separate macOS `go vet` job is not needed (lint already vets); do not add one unless the Windows reasoning (native vet coverage) clearly applies to darwin-only files — if it does, say so and add it.
3. Update tests: extend the harness unit tests for the new target (plan/inventory/verify for darwin; the POSIX command-line budget; binary naming) and update `tests/test_workflow_contract.py` so it pins the new macOS jobs as strictly as it pins the Windows ones. Make sure the job that runs the harness unit tests in CI still runs them.
4. Preserve semantics: the macOS shards together must run exactly the set of tests that `go test ./...` runs on darwin today — every default-runnable root of the heavy packages exactly once, every other package once — with the same env/lifecycle details the README lists (PWD, GOTOOLDIR on PATH, -test.paniconexit0, 30m package timeout, shuffle off, no forced -parallel/GOMAXPROCS). Anything that cannot be preserved must fail closed, as on Windows.

Verification you MUST do — this machine is darwin/arm64, so run the real thing locally, not just unit tests:
- `python3 -B -m unittest discover -s tools/ci-bench/windows-production/tests -p "test_*.py"` (or the new location) passes.
- Run the macOS flow end to end locally against this worktree at its committed HEAD: prepare → run each shard → run non-heavy packages → verify, using a temp output dir under the worktree's parent temp (not inside the repo). The harness requires a clean tracked worktree and an unchanged commit, so commit first. Report the wall time of prepare, of each shard, of the non-heavy run, and the verifier result. Shards may be run sequentially locally. If Go's default 10-minute timeout or machine load interferes, say so; the harness's own 30m timeout should apply.
- Check the workflow file parses (e.g. `python3 -c "import yaml,sys; yaml.safe_load(open('.github/workflows/test.yml'))"` if PyYAML is available, or `actionlint` if installed — do not install tools; say what you could not check).
- `go vet ./...` and `gofmt -l` for any Go you touch (inventory_testmain.go).

To locate code/relations in the repo you may use `entire graph query --repo . --profile full --format agent --max-context-bytes 4096 --query "..."` (grep is fine for literal strings and for YAML/Python; fall back to reading source if a graph command fails).

Commit in logical commits (harness generalisation; macOS settings/weights; workflow; tests/docs), each message ending with the line `Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>`.

Report back (under 500 words): the design you chose (what is shared vs per-target) and why; files changed; commit hashes; the exact commands you ran and their real results, including the local end-to-end timings and verifier outcome; expected CI wall time for macOS and what it is bounded by; anything you could not verify locally (the GitHub macOS runner differs from this machine: core count, artifact upload/download, permissions on downloaded test binaries such as the executable bit being lost by actions/upload-artifact — handle that explicitly); and open risks or follow-ups (e.g. how to enable the same for Linux).

input.command:
git status --short | head -3; git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD; git diff --stat origin/main..HEAD | tail -1; git push -u origin ci/macos-test-shards 2>&1 | tail -1 && gh pr create --base main --head ci/macos-test-shards --title "ci: shard the macOS test job with the Windows harness" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Problem

In the `test` workflow every job finishes within about 9 minutes except `test (macos-latest)`, which runs `go test -timeout 30m ./...` as a single job on the GitHub-hosted macOS runner and takes 17–20 minutes. It alone roughly doubles CI wall time on every PR.

## Change

The macOS test job is now sharded through the same harness Windows already uses (`tools/ci-bench/windows-production/`).

**Harness**
- A new `targets.py` holds everything that differs per target. Every script takes `--target`, defaulting to `windows/amd64`, so the Windows invocations are unchanged. The target must agree with the settings, the host platform, `go env` and every artifact, or the step fails closed.
- macOS has its own `settings.darwin-arm64.json` (4 shards, the same three heavy packages, `*.test` binaries) and `historical-weights.darwin-arm64.json`, seeded from one local M1 run.
- The POSIX command-line budget is 262144 argv bytes, a quarter of macOS `ARG_MAX`. Each launch also checks argv plus environment against `sysconf(SC_ARG_MAX)`, and the verifier requires that record.
- `run_shard.py` restores the executable bit on downloaded test binaries after their SHA-256 matches the plan, since artifact transport drops it.

**Workflow**
- New jobs mirror the Windows ones: compile and plan, shards, non-heavy packages, vet, coverage and integrity.
- An aggregate job keeps the required check name `test (macos-latest)`.
- `test (ubuntu-latest)` is unchanged.
- macOS uses 4 shards, not 8: GitHub-hosted macOS concurrency is limited and this workflow already runs other macOS jobs.
- A native macOS `go vet` job is added because darwin/BSD-only files exist, lint vets only Linux, and the harness compiles with `-vet=off`.

## Verification

Run locally on darwin/arm64 at the branch head:
- Harness unit tests: 68 pass (35 before).
- The Windows fixture produces byte-identical `plan.json`, inventories and settings with the old and new code.
- `actionlint` with shellcheck is clean apart from the unknown `depot-*` runner labels.
- Full macOS flow end to end, with the execute bit stripped from the binaries to simulate artifact transport: prepare 35 s cold, shards 255 s / 249 s / 209 s / 170 s, non-heavy packages 10 s, verifier passed with 3811 roots each run exactly once and 21 non-heavy packages.
- Removing one shard's evidence, or verifying as the Windows target, fails as intended.

Not verified locally, so this PR's own CI run is the test:
- The modified harness on Windows. It has only run on darwin.
- The GitHub macOS runner: core count, `setup-python`, and the real artifact round trip.

## Expected effect

macOS should drop from 17–20 minutes to roughly 10–13. That is an estimate from local timings, not a measurement. The slowest shard is bounded by two `internal/cli` tests of about 160–170 s each, so more shards would not help until those are split.

## Risks and follow-ups

- With the vet job, five macOS jobs start at once (build, statusline, prompt-context-hook, compile-and-plan, vet). If the account's macOS concurrency cap is 5, folding vet into the non-heavy job would free a runner.
- The weights come from one M1 run and should be refreshed from CI shard evidence.
- Linux could use the same harness with a `targets.py` entry and a settings file; Ubuntu is at about 5 minutes today, so it is not the limit.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -1

The macOS sharding port is done and open as [#402](https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/pull/402). Its own CI run is the real test, and I'm watching it now (ignoring Entire Gates).

**What it does**

- The Windows harness is now target-generic: a new `targets.py` holds everything platform-specific, and every script takes a `--target` that defaults to Windows, so the Windows jobs are invoked exactly as before.
- macOS gets the same job layout as Windows: compile and plan, 4 shards, non-heavy packages, a verifier, and an aggregate job that keeps the required check name `test (macos-latest)`.
- A native macOS `go vet` job is added, because darwin-only files exist and the existing lint job vets only Linux.

**Verified locally on this Mac**

- The harness unit tests pass: 68, up from 35.
- The Windows test fixture produces byte-identical plans with the old and new code.
- The full macOS flow ran end to end, with the execute bit stripped from the binaries to simulate artifact transport: shards took 255, 249, 209 and 170 seconds, and the verifier confirmed all 3,811 tests ran exactly once.

**Not verified until CI finishes**

- The modified harness on Windows; it has only run on macOS so far.
- GitHub's macOS runner: core count and the real artifact round trip.

**Expected gain:** macOS from 17–20 minutes down to roughly 10–13. That is an estimate from local timings. The slowest shard is bounded by two `internal/cli` tests of about 160–170 seconds each, so more shards won't help until those are split.

**One risk:** with the new vet job, five macOS jobs start at once. If your account's macOS concurrency cap is 5, jobs will queue; folding vet into the non-heavy job would free a runner.

I'll report the actual CI timings when the run completes.
