content.text:
CI on #402 is fully green: all 43 checks pass (leaving Entire Gates to you), and the `test` workflow finished in 12 min 25 s, down from about 20.

**macOS, as measured on GitHub's runner**

| Job | Time |
|---|---|
| Compile and plan | 2 min 49 s |
| Shards | 6 min 12 s, 7 min 1 s, 8 min 37 s, 9 min 2 s |
| Non-heavy packages | 1 min 12 s |
| Vet | 2 min 31 s |
| Coverage and integrity | 19 s |
| **`test (macos-latest)` done** | **12 min 24 s after trigger** |

So macOS dropped from 17–20 minutes to about 12.5, inside the 10–13 minute estimate. The shards ran about twice as slowly on GitHub's runner as on this Mac, as expected with fewer cores. No queueing showed up: all five macOS jobs started within seconds, so the concurrency cap was not hit on this run.

**Windows on the modified harness** passed, which was the main thing not verified locally. But it took 12 min 6 s here against about 9 min on the earlier #389 run:

- Compile and plan took 4 min 8 s, up from 2 min 38 s.
- Shard 0 took 7 min 31 s, up from 3 min 38 s; the other shards were about the same as before.

I can't tell from one run whether that is runner variance or something the port changed. The shard plan is byte-identical for the same inputs, which points to variance, but it is worth comparing against the next run or two before concluding.

**Where the time goes now:** macOS and Windows both finish at about 12 minutes, so they are jointly the limit. Getting lower would need two things:

- Splitting the two slow `internal/cli` tests that bound the slowest macOS shard.
- Shortening the compile-and-plan step that every shard waits on (about 3–4 minutes on both platforms).

#402 is ready for your review. #389 is also still waiting on your approval, and #399 is next after that.

Next phase on the macOS sharding work: drive the `test` workflow's wall time as low as you can. Your branch is pushed and open as PR #402 (https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/pull/402); its first CI run was fully green in 745 s total (was ~1200 s). The maintainer said: "Keep going, the shorter the better."

Measured on that run (seconds; "done" = after trigger):
- macOS: compile-and-plan 169 (done 173); shards 372 / 421 / 517 / 542 (last done 718); non-heavy 72; vet 151; verify 19 (done 737); aggregate done 744. All five initial macOS jobs started within seconds — no queueing observed.
- Windows: compile-and-plan 248 (done 250; it was 158 on an earlier run on main); shards 225–284 except shard 1 = 397 and shard 0 = 451 (done 702; on the earlier run shard 0 was 218 and shard 1 was 371); non-heavy 169; vet 233; verify 23 (done 726).
- test (ubuntu-latest): 327 as a single job. CodeQL (separate workflow) ~390.
So both macOS and Windows end at ~12 min, each = compile-and-plan + slowest shard + verify.

You are now allowed to push to `origin ci/macos-test-shards` (that branch ONLY; normal fast-forward pushes, no force, no other branches, no PR edits/comments) so you can iterate against real CI. Watch runs with `gh run list --workflow test.yml --branch ci/macos-test-shards` / `gh run view <id> --json jobs` (per-job and per-step timings are in the jobs JSON) and `gh run download` for shard evidence artifacts. IGNORE the "Entire Gates" check entirely — it is the maintainer's manual approval; never wait on it (do not use a bare `gh pr checks --watch`). Each CI round costs ~10 min, so batch changes sensibly; aim for at most ~4 rounds, and stop earlier when the remaining gain is small.

Start by getting facts, not guesses: pull the per-STEP timings for the compile-and-plan jobs and for one shard job on each platform from the green run (checkout, setup-go incl. cache restore, setup-python, harness unit tests, compile, artifact upload/download, test execution), and the per-root timings from the shard evidence artifacts.

Levers, roughly by expected payoff — verify each with data before and after:
1. Shard balance. The spread (macOS 372→542, Windows 225→451) says the weights are off. Refresh `historical-weights*.json` for BOTH targets from the real CI shard evidence of the green run (and write/extend a small script in the harness dir that regenerates weights from downloaded evidence, with a unit test, so this is repeatable; document it in the README). A balanced plan should bring the slowest shard near the mean.
2. Shard count on macOS. With accurate weights, test whether more macOS shards (6, then 8) reduce the slowest shard without queueing; look at each job's queued→started gap to detect the account's macOS concurrency cap. If jobs queue, back off to the largest count that does not, and record the finding in the settings comment/README. Folding the macOS vet job into the non-heavy job as a step is acceptable if it frees a runner that matters.
3. The floor set by single slow roots. On macOS the slowest shard is bounded by the longest top-level tests in `internal/cli` (`TestAgentSearchExactNameAnchorsOnTheSignatureAcrossLanguages` ~170 s and `TestAgentSearchExactNameNeverDropsVerify` ~159 s on an M1, roughly double on the hosted runner). Look at why they are slow; if they are table tests over languages/cases, split them into several top-level tests (or otherwise restructure) so the planner can spread them — WITHOUT weakening what they assert and without changing production code. Do the same for any other root that alone exceeds ~half the target shard time on either platform. Run the affected tests locally before pushing.
4. Fixed overhead before and around the shards. Whatever the step timings show: e.g. shard jobs restoring a large Go build cache they do not need (they run prebuilt binaries — consider `cache: false` on setup-go in shard jobs if the harness only needs the toolchain), running the harness unit tests inside the critical-path prepare job (move them to their own parallel job if they cost real time, keeping them required via the aggregate), artifact compression level/size, whether compile-and-plan gets a warm build cache on PR runs (cache key/restore-keys), and whether the compile step can build the three test binaries in parallel. Only change what the data says matters.
5. `test (ubuntu-latest)` at ~330 s becomes part of the limit once the others drop below it. If and only if macOS and Windows get under ~6 min, consider adding a linux/amd64 target to the harness (you estimated: a targets.py entry, a settings file, a per-argument MAX_ARG_STRLEN check) while keeping the required check name `test (ubuntu-latest)` via an aggregate job. Otherwise leave Linux alone and just report it.

Constraints that do not bend: the verifier must still prove every default-runnable root ran exactly once and every non-heavy package once, on every target; required check names `test (macos-latest)`, `test (windows-latest)`, `test (ubuntu-latest)` must keep existing and must fail if any component fails; Windows behaviour must stay correct (it is now exercised by CI on this branch — check its jobs every round); no weakening of tests, no skipping, no `-short`, no forced `-parallel`/GOMAXPROCS changes to test semantics; harness unit tests and `tests/test_workflow_contract.py` updated to match; `actionlint` clean; commit messages end with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>`. Do not run `entire session ...` / `entire enable|disable|clean|auth`.

Report back (under 500 words): a before/after table per CI round (total workflow wall time; per platform: compile-and-plan, slowest shard, mean shard, done-after-trigger), what you changed in each round and why, what the data showed did NOT help, any macOS concurrency cap you observed, the final green run's id and timings, commit hashes, and what now bounds the wall time (so the maintainer knows what the next lever would be).
